title.en: Reshaping India's political map: 13th to 18th century

text.en: Imagine a map of India in 1200 and another in 1700. The borders, kingdoms and capitals are all different. This chapter follows how India's political map changed.

From the 13th century, many invasions by peoples from Central Asia, often Turkic or Afghan, led to new powers in India.
The Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 and was ruled by dynasties like the Mamluks (Slave dynasty), Khaljis, Tughluqs, Sayyids and Lodis.
The Vijayanagara Empire, founded in the 14th century in the south, built the great city of Hampi and ruled for over two centuries.
In 1565 the Battle of Talikota led to the defeat of Vijayanagara and the destruction of its capital city.
In 1526 Babur won the First Battle of Panipat and began the Mughal Empire.
The Mughal empire grew under emperors like Akbar, who built a strong administration, and it reached its widest extent under Aurangzeb.
The Ahoms of Assam resisted the Mughals and won the Battle of Saraighat in 1671.
Many regional kingdoms also rose, such as the Rajputs, Sikhs, Marathas and Nawabs of Bengal and Awadh.
Historians use the word medieval, meaning between two ages, for this period, though India's history is very different from Europe's.
By the mid-18th century Maratha power spread across large parts of India and the Mughal power weakened.

problem.en: Arrange in time order: Battle of Talikota, First Battle of Panipat, Battle of Saraighat.

text.en: First Battle of Panipat is in 1526.

prompt.en: Why did India's political map keep changing?

requiredIdeas.en: New powers invaded and new dynasties rose.

points.en: The Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and the Mughals changed the political map.
